name: Matabei-zakura

location.address: Honmura, Ouda, Uda City, Nara Prefecture

access: Free, standing on the former Goto family samurai residence site; open ground with no gate or entry fee (parking only is charged, about 500 yen, during peak bloom).
transport: Kintetsu Osaka Line to Haibara Station, then Nara Kotsu bus toward Oudakoko-mae (Ouda High School front), about 20 minutes, then roughly 20 minutes on foot.
verify_notes: A famous weeping cherry (shidarezakura), also called Taki-zakura (Waterfall Cherry), in Uda City's Ouda ward, Nara Prefecture (town: Uda, not Nara city; roughly 25km/well outside Nara's cluster, matches the brief's note this belongs to an Uda-area page rather than Nara). Both sources give height 13m and trunk girth 'over 3 metres' (used girth_cm 300 as a floor; exact figure beyond that not given, so treated as approximate). Age is consistently reported as 'said to be about 300 years' (both sources use hedged phrasing, 'とも言われる'/'とも'), not a growth-rate calculation, so kept broad and flagged rather than stated as precise. Name comes from Goto Matabei (Goto Mototsugu), a Sengoku-era general who reportedly settled in Ouda after the fall of the Toyotomi clan; the tree stands on the site of his family's former residence. Nara Prefecture protected tree. Featured in the opening credits of NHK's 2000 taiga drama 'Aoi: Tokugawa Sandai'. Night-illuminated during peak bloom (early-mid April). One collectible point, clearly the destination (a named, signposted single tree with its own local festival, Matabei-zakura Matsuri).

name: Sen'nen-zakura of Butsuryuji
species: Mochizuki Cherry (Prunus x, a Yamazakura x Edohigan hybrid)

location.address: Butsuryuji temple, Akahani 1684, Haibara, Uda City, Nara Prefecture

access: Paid entry: 200 yen temple grounds entry (plus 300 yen if also visiting the main hall), with an optional 100 yen conservation donation for the cherry tree itself. Free parking (about 10 spaces) at the temple.
transport: Kintetsu Osaka Line to Haibara Station, then Nara Kotsu bus to Takaishita stop (about 16 min), then roughly 40 minutes / 2.2km on foot; or about 5 minutes by car from the Takaigosaki intersection on Route 369.
verify_notes: Stands beside the stone steps of Butsuryuji temple's approach path (Haibara area of Uda City, NOT the same district as Matabei-zakura, which is in Ouda; both fall inside Uda City so both belong on the same place page as far as the municipality goes). Sources agree closely: trunk circumference 7.7m, height 16m, splitting into 11 large and small limbs from about 2m above the base, over 900 years old, 'the largest and oldest cherry tree in Nara Prefecture'. Designated a Nara Prefecture Natural Monument (official register status, counts as one of the two sources). Age is the register/tourist-board's own repeated claim, not a growth-rate derivation by us, so flagged as an inherited estimate rather than independently verified; a Prunus this old is itself remarkable (most cherries do not live anywhere near 900 years) so the age claim, while extraordinary, is the one consistently used by the prefecture and every source found, with no disagreement across sources. The Commons photo caption's '1000-year-old cherry tree' (Sen'nen = 'thousand year') is the popular nickname rather than the measured age; used the sourced 'over 900 years' instead of the rounder folk number, per the rule not to trust a filename/nickname over what a real source says. Species is Mochizuki-zakura, a locally named hybrid cultivar; genus is Prunus. Night-illuminated during peak bloom (early-mid April) until 9pm.

name: Yatsufusa Sugi

location.address: Sakurami Shrine, Utano-Sakura, Uda City, Nara Prefecture (postcode 633-2224)

access: Free, on the grounds of Sakurami Shrine (public shrine precinct, open ground, no fee or gate mentioned by any source).
transport: Kintetsu Osaka Line to Haibara Station, then a bus toward the Utano area followed by roughly a 60-minute walk; or by car via National Routes 369/166 and Nara Prefectural Road 31 from the Hari interchange of the Nara Expressway.
verify_notes: Third district of Uda City (Utano, distinct from Ouda and Haibara where the other two Uda trees stand; all three are still inside Uda City). A cluster of fused cedar trunks growing from one base beside Sakurami Shrine's shrine building (a National Natural Monument, kunishitei tennen kinenbutsu, designated 25 April 1932, the strongest Japanese heritage tier, above the prefectural designation the other two Uda trees carry). SOURCE CONFLICT, flagged rather than resolved: the official Nara prefectural tourism site (nara-kankou.or.jp) gives 8 trunks and a base circumference of 9m (900cm, used as girth_cm); Japanese Wikipedia gives 6 trunks (one felled by a 1979 typhoon but still living), height about 20m, and a combined girth of 13.5m measured by summing each trunk's own circumference (individually 1.2m to 8.4m) rather than one base measurement, which likely explains part of the gap versus the 9m base figure. Both agree the trunks are fused at the base and intertwine ('reclining dragon' growth form) and that this odd growth form is exactly why Miyoshi Sakuichi got it designated in 1932 ('academic value'). AGE: no real source gives one. Nara tourism repeats only a legend that it was planted when Emperor Jinmu camped there during the legendary pacification of Yamato (i.e. no date at all, folklore rather than evidence); left age_estimate empty rather than repeat a myth as a figure, and this is exactly the case the brief says should ask the reader. Held up since at least the 1970s/80s by steel cables anchored in concrete (visible in both supplied photos, matches the 1979 storm-damage note), cost split between national government, prefecture, city and the shrine, upkeep now a struggle given the shrinking local population per Wikipedia.
